answer.label: Not Henry Ford — an unsourced modern paraphrase
answer.authorName: No verified author (misattributed to Henry Ford)
answer.authorDates: Ford lived 1863–1947; the line was first tied to him only in 2001
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Henry Ford ever said or wrote this. It appears in none of his books or authenticated interviews, and The Henry Ford museum itself lists it as misattributed ↗. The earliest attribution to Ford that Quote Investigator could find ↗ is a 2001 letter to Marketing Week — 54 years after Ford’s death — making this a piece of modern business folklore, not a documented Ford quotation.

source.excerpt: “If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found no compelling evidence Ford said it; the earliest direct ascription is a 2001 letter to Marketing Week, while the underlying concept only evolved over decades with an initial related cite by 1930.
The Henry Ford museum ↗ states the line “has never been satisfactorily traced to Henry Ford” and only emerged in the early 21st century among business writers.
Check Your Fact ↗ rated it False: it does not appear in Ford’s autobiography My Life and Work nor on the museum’s list of 200+ verified Ford quotations.
source.excerptNote: A near-identical variant — “If I had asked my customers what they wanted they would have said a faster horse” — circulates alongside it; neither wording has been traced to Ford.

author.name: Henry Ford
author.heading: About Henry Ford
author.bio: Henry Ford (1863–1947) founded the Ford Motor Company and popularized moving-assembly-line mass production, making the Model T affordable to ordinary Americans. He co-authored several books with ghostwriter Samuel Crowther, including My Life and Work (1922). Despite his fame as an innovator, this widely shared line about “faster horses” does not appear in any of his authenticated writings or interviews.

misattribution.heading: Why this one is misattributed
misattribution.intro: The quote is one of the internet’s most-shared “innovation” lines, but no version of it can be traced to Henry Ford during his lifetime.

items.why: The line is absent from Ford’s autobiography My Life and Work and from the Henry Ford museum’s list of 200+ verified quotations ↗. The earliest attribution to Ford is a 2001 letter to Marketing Week ↗, 54 years after his death.

The Henry Ford museum ↗ notes the saying “only emerged in the early 21st century” among business writers using it as a lesson; related expressions about breeding faster horses date back to the 1930s but were never Ford’s words.

misattribution.truthLine: No documented source ties this line to Henry Ford; Quote Investigator ↗ and The Henry Ford ↗ both treat it as an unverified, modern attribution.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The “faster horses” line thrives because it flatters a comfortable idea: that visionary founders should ignore customer research and trust their own genius. It is quoted in pitch decks, design talks and strategy books as shorthand for “users don’t know what they want.”

Ironically, the historical Ford is on record making almost the opposite point — that success lies in seeing things from the other person’s point of view — which is one reason historians treat the pithy anti-research version as a later invention rather than his own words.
context.pull: Absent from his books, his interviews, and the museum’s verified list — the line surfaces only in the 21st century.
